title: Mirabel and the Language
premise: Petra Okonkwo, a translator who has spent a decade refusing to speak her mother's dying language aloud, is summoned by Nana Adaeze, the language's last fluent speaker, to become her final student. As lessons deepen, Petra uncovers why her family arranged itself around silence: her mother, memory dissolving from early dementia, once made a vow that cost Petra her name in that tongue. When Nana Adaeze's health fails and the mother's memory nears its end, Petra must finally ask the forbidden question—what was promised, and by whom—and choose whether love means preserving a language or letting it rest. The novel ends with Petra speaking the language aloud at two bedsides, one hearing it for the last time, one perhaps for the first.
about_author: Jonah Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent years listening to what people almost said. They write about inheritance, silence, and the families we build around unspeakable things, and live between two cities and three languages.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Word
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. In her London translation office, Petra catches herself substituting an English word where her mother's tongue should be, and realizes she has done this ten thousand times. A client's gratitude feels like theft. Emotional beat: quiet grief disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: A Letter in a Dying Hand
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. A letter arrives from Nana Adaeze, an elderly woman Petra has never met, asking her to come as final student of a language with no other speakers left. Petra drafts refusals all night. Beat: fear dressed as inconvenience.

chapters.title: What Mother Still Says
chapters.summary: Petra visits her mother Grace in a care home; Grace drifts between English and fragments of their shared tongue, sometimes calling Petra by a name Petra doesn't recognize. Beat: tenderness laced with dread.

chapters.title: The House of One Speaker
chapters.summary: Petra travels to the coastal town where Nana Adaeze lives among labeled objects—every noun annotated like a museum exhibit. The old woman tests her with a greeting Petra refuses to answer. Beat: wary mutual recognition.

chapters.title: First Lesson, First Refusal
chapters.summary: Nana Adaeze begins teaching; Petra can translate anything written but freezes when asked to speak. The old woman says silence is also a sentence. Beat: frustration curdling into shame.

chapters.title: Chidi
chapters.summary: Petra meets Chidi, Nana Adaeze's grandnephew, a local teacher who records the lessons and jokes easily. His warmth unsettles her more than the lessons do. Beat: reluctant hope.

chapters.title: The Vow, Overheard
chapters.summary: Nana Adaeze's POV. The old woman remembers the night decades ago when Grace, then a young woman, came to her in tears and asked her never to teach Petra. She agreed, and has regretted it since. Beat: guilt across generations.

chapters.title: Words That Don't Translate
chapters.summary: Lessons continue through objects and stories; Petra learns words for grief, debt, and homecoming that have no English equivalents. She writes them down without saying them. Beat: hunger she won't admit.

chapters.title: Grace Forgets a Tuesday
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Her mother fails to recognize her during a phone call, then recovers mid-sentence into perfect fluency in the old tongue. Petra realizes time is running out on both fronts. Beat: panic beneath composure.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Chidi shows Petra his archive: hours of Nana Adaeze's voice, songs, prayers, arguments. He asks why someone so fluent refuses to make sound. Petra walks out. Beat: confrontation as intimacy.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Alone, Petra practices a single word at the sea wall and cannot finish it. Flashback to age twelve, the day her mother slapped a word out of her mouth and said 'we don't use that here.' Beat: the wound named.

chapters.title: Nana Adaeze Falls
chapters.summary: The old woman collapses mid-lesson; hospital waits and paperwork follow. Chidi and Petra keep vigil together, translating for nurses, becoming a small unit. Beat: found family forming under pressure.

chapters.title: The Question Arranged Around
chapters.summary: In the hospital corridor, Petra finally asks Chidi directly: why would my mother forbid this? He admits he knows only that there was a promise, witnessed, before Petra was born. Beat: the mystery sharpened.

chapters.title: Grace's Good Day
chapters.summary: Petra brings recordings of Nana Adaeze to her mother. Grace listens, lucid for an hour, and begins to tell the story—then stops herself, terrified, saying 'ask her, not me.' Beat: hope deferred.

chapters.title: The Witness
chapters.summary: Nana Adaeze, discharged and frail, decides the truth matters more than the promise. She tells Petra: Grace swore the language away to protect Petra from a father's family who claimed the tongue as property—a custody war fought in vocabulary. Beat: revelation reframing everything.

chapters.title: Anger, Translated
chapters.summary: Petra rages—at her mother, at Nana Adaeze for obeying, at herself for a decade of self-erasure mistaken for loyalty. Chidi stays anyway. Beat: rupture before repair.

chapters.title: Two Bedsides
chapters.summary: Grace deteriorates sharply; Nana Adaeze weakens in parallel. Petra shuttles between hospitals, keeping both women alive to each other through letters read aloud. Beat: love against duty, literally enacted.

chapters.title: The Word at Last
chapters.summary: Climax. At Grace's bedside, Petra speaks the forbidden word—the childhood name—in full voice. Grace answers in the old tongue, calling her daughter home. Beat: catharsis; the silence broken.

chapters.title: What the Last Speaker Leaves
chapters.summary: Nana Adaeze, knowing her time is short, formally passes the language to Petra—not as ownership but as obligation: 'a language is a guest; feed it.' Beat: succession, weight accepted.

chapters.title: The Funeral in Two Languages
chapters.summary: Nana Adaeze dies. At the funeral, Petra delivers part of the eulogy in the tongue everyone assumed was finished; strangers approach afterward asking to learn. Beat: grief transmuted into continuity.

chapters.title: Teaching the Kitchen Table
chapters.summary: Petra moves her mother nearer, hires help, and begins teaching a small circle—Chidi, two neighbors, eventually children—at her kitchen table. Grace attends, forgetting details but remembering sounds. Beat: quiet rebuilding.

chapters.title: Mirabel
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Petra's POV. Grace, near the end, calls her Mirabel again—the name in the old tongue—and Petra answers to it, out loud, without flinching. The language survives not intact but alive, carried in a changed voice. Beat: resolution; love chosen over duty, memory over silence.
